speaker: Doctor
text: Since test requests are currently unavailable, I will rely on your description. Does the pain radiate to your jaw or teeth, and have you noticed any clicking sounds or limited movement in your jaw joint?

speaker: Patient
text: No, the pain doesn't radiate to my jaw or teeth, and I haven't noticed any clicking or limited movement in my jaw joint. It seems isolated to the ear itself when I chew.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any pain or discomfort when you press on the area just in front of your ear, where the jaw joint is located? Also, have you noticed any swelling or redness around the earring piercing site?

speaker: Patient
text: No, pressing on the area in front of my ear doesn't cause any pain. However, I do feel significant discomfort and tenderness when I wear earrings.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the tenderness at the piercing site and the history of recent surgery, I suspect a localized infection or foreign body reaction. Do you see any redness, swelling, or discharge coming from the earring piercing itself?

speaker: Patient
text: I don't see any redness, swelling, or discharge coming from the piercing site itself. The discomfort is just a general sensitivity when the earring is in place.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since there are no signs of infection, the sensitivity to earrings and pain with chewing suggests irritation of the auricular branch of the vagus nerve or the facial nerve. Do you experience any dizziness, hearing changes, or a sensation of fullness in the ear when the pain occurs?

speaker: Patient
text: I don't experience any dizziness or a sensation of fullness in my ear. My hearing actually improved by 20 decibels according to my audiology report from last week.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since your hearing has improved and there are no signs of infection or TMJ dysfunction, the pain with chewing and earring sensitivity likely stems from nerve irritation or scar tissue formation near the ear canal. Do you have any history of metal allergies, and does the pain change if you switch to hypoallergenic earrings?

speaker: Patient
text: I don't have a known history of metal allergies, and I haven't tried switching to hypoallergenic earrings yet. The pain seems to come and go regardless of what I'm wearing, mostly triggered by the act of chewing.

speaker: Doctor
text: Since the pain is triggered by chewing rather than the earring material, this points toward referred pain from the temporomandibular joint or the tragus. Does the pain occur specifically when you press on the tragus, the small flap of cartilage at the front of the ear canal?

speaker: Patient
text: Yes, pressing on the tragus does trigger that same sharp, shooting pain. It feels very sensitive to touch in that specific spot.

speaker: Doctor
text: This specific tenderness at the tragus, combined with pain triggered by chewing, strongly suggests irritation of the auriculotemporal nerve or a neuroma at the surgical site. Have you noticed any numbness or tingling in the skin over the temple or cheek on that same side?

speaker: Patient
text: No, I haven't noticed any numbness or tingling in my temple or cheek. The sensation is strictly limited to that sharp pain in the ear when I eat or touch the tragus.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the tragus tenderness and pain with chewing without sensory loss, I suspect auriculotemporal neuralgia or a small neuroma. DIAGNOSIS READY: Auriculotemporal Neuralgia
